previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of morbid obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, COPD, chronic diastolic heart failure, and tobacco use was admitted for lethargy and hypoxia. She had been increasingly somnolent and was found with low oxygen levels, improving with supplemental oxygen. Chest imaging showed moderate pulmonary edema contributing to her respiratory compromise, and she was treated with IV furosemide. She remained noncompliant with CPAP use during admission and declined smoking cessation. Her metabolic encephalopathy improved with supportive care. She was discharged home with services, on unchanged medications, with strong recommendations to use CPAP and stop smoking to reduce readmission risk.

Brief Hospital Course:
This is a ___ female h/o dCHF (EF 55%), COPD, obesity 
hypoventilation, OSA with CPAP (almost no compliance) now here 
with chest pain that has resolved on arrival here as well as 
hypoxia.

# Respiratory failure: likely multifactorial, including COPD 
exacerbation (tight on exam) potential pneumonia contributing 
(fever and cough, though CXR not entirely convincing), dCHF with 
volume overload (pulm edema on CXR). This overlies chronic 
issues of obesity hypoventilation syndrome and OSA (noncompliant 
with CPAP). Patient with negative troponin x3 ruling out ACS. 
Patient was intubated overnight ___ for increased work of 
breathing, then successfully extubated ___. She was continued 
on duonebs q6 hrs and albuterol q2 hours prn. She was initially 
treated with IV solumedrol which was subsequently transitioned 
to po prednisone. She was also initially started on antibiotics 
for HCAP given fever, respiratory distress, and leukocytosis. 
However, given clinical improvement and lack of consolidation on 
CXR, antibiotics were changed to levofloxacin for COPD 
exacerbation. 
She was transferred to the floor early in the morning on ___, 
but returned later in the morning due to hypoxemia ___ to 
nonadherence to oxygen by NC and somnolence with pCO2 ranging 
from ___ torr.
.
The patient was sent back to the ICU due to this hypoxia where 
she was stabilized again on a nasal cannula, and over the course 
of 2 additional days she had significant improvement in her 
mental status, ambulatory status, and most importantly, 
improvement in her respiratory status, maintaining o2 
saturations in the low ___.  She does have dyspnea on exertion, 
but this is baseline for the patient.
.
# UTI  urine culture shows >100K MDR E. Coli. Patient was 
started on treatment with meropenem. However, repeat UA and 
urine culture showed no infection, so the meropenem was stopped 
___.
.
# Agitation: Initial presentation consistent with delirium in 
the setting of infection, hypoxia.  Also, pt has h/o agitation 
and noncompliance at baseline. While in the MICU patient was 
intermittently put in wrist restraints and treated with IV 
haldol for her agitation. 
.
# dCHF: Initially held beta blocker and ACE given SBPs in low 
100s with propofol. Her ACEi and beta blocker were gradually 
added back as pressures stabilized.  

# CAD/HTN: Initially held ACE, beta blocker, spironolactone, 
isosorbide. Her plavix was continued. She was gradually 
restarted on her home medications. 
.
# Depression: continued home aripiprazole, fluoxetine  
.
# DMII: on metformin at home. Blood sugars were controlled with 
insulin sliding scale while in house. 
.
# Chest pain: resolved on arrival to ED. EKG similar to 
baseline. Trop negative x 3.

Discharge Instructions:
It was a pleasure caring for you Ms ___. 

You have congestive heart failure and will tend to accumulate 
fluid if you're not careful. Please weigh yourself every 
morning, call MD if weight goes up more than 3 lbs.

You were seen in the hospital for a worsening of your chronic 
lung disease.  Your disease had reached a critical point and in 
order to help you breath, you needed to have a breathing tube 
placed in your airway.  This was removed after one day.  Also, 
you stayed in the intensive care unit for most of your stay; 
this was due to the severity of your disease.  Eventually your 
breathing returned to what is likely your baseline, you still 
require oxygen.  You should avoid smoking at all costs.  
Nicotine patches can be provided.  You do not need any 
additional antibiotics at this time.
.
The following changes are being made to your medications:

START prednisone (5mg pills) everyday for 2 weeks as directed
START nicotine patch everyday when not smoking
START albuterol nebulizer every 6 hours
START albuterol nebulizer every 2 hours as needed
START ipratropium bromide nebulizer every 6 hours
STOP isosorbide mononitrate
STOP spironolactone
STOP albuterol sulfate inhaler

You have chronic respiratory problems that are in part due to 
obstructive sleep apnea. You can improve your breathing problems 
by using a CPAP machine every night. You also have low oxygen 
levels and will live longer if you wear oxygen.

Smoking is very bad for your health, especially given all of 
your breathing problems. You will live longer and spend less 
time in the hospital if you quit smoking.
